name: Raw milk for height

lead: Raw milk for height is the practice of drinking unpasteurised milk in the hope of growing taller. Followers in some height-focused communities see it as a nutrient-dense food that supports growth and immunity.

The chain is nutrition: protein and other milk nutrients are supplied, growth is supported, and final height benefits. Reference sources report that populations eating more dairy and animal protein tend to be taller, without separating raw from pasteurised milk, and they report that heating does not substantially change milk's nutritional value. No study of raw milk and height was found.

paras: People drink it as a daily food, often alongside other nutrition-focused height routines, and usually start in the teen years while growth is still possible. Supporters source it from farms where it is legal. Any effect on height would show up over years of growth, not weeks.

The CDC and FDA recommend against raw milk because it can carry pathogens such as Listeria, Salmonella and E. coli, with the highest risk in young children, older adults, pregnancy and weakened immunity. Outbreaks are documented. Legal status varies by country and US state.

angle.text: Some height-focused communities drink raw milk to supply protein and nutrients for growth and end up taller. Dairy-rich diets track with taller populations in reference sources, but no study has looked at raw milk and height specifically.

lead: Raw milk for height is the practice of drinking unpasteurised milk in the hope of growing taller or filling out one's frame. It appears in height-focused and looksmaxxing circles alongside slogans such as "Raw Milk + Healthy = Holy Height", and is often grouped with primal and carnivore-style diets. The appearance goal is straightforward: milk supplies protein, calcium and fat-soluble vitamins, and adherents treat it as a growth-supporting food for people who are still growing.[1][2]

Dairy and height are linked at the population level. Wikipedia's article on human height reports that nations eating more protein from meat, dairy, eggs and fish tend to be taller than those relying on cereal protein, and that historically cattle-rich, high-dairy populations were taller.[3] That association concerns dairy generally, not raw milk specifically. Twin studies put the heritability of height at roughly 60 to 80 percent, and growth typically ends in the late teens.[3]

Raw milk itself is milk that has not been heat-treated. Proponents say it tastes better, is more nutritious and supports immunity.[4] A 2011 systematic review and meta-analysis of 40 studies on vitamins found that pasteurisation lowered some vitamins (B1, B2, C, folate) while the overall effect on nutritive value was reported as minimal, and it did not find support for several advocacy claims.[5] The CDC and FDA advise against drinking raw milk because it can carry pathogens, and legal access varies by country and US state.[4] No published study has measured height outcomes in people drinking raw versus pasteurised milk.

paras: Raw milk is milk sold or consumed without pasteurisation. Wikipedia reports that proponents credit it with better flavour, more nutrition, immune support and protection against allergies.[4] In looksmaxxing forums the milk is usually discussed together with raw meat, liver and eggs as part of a primal-diet approach, and sometimes as a way to improve skin, hormones or bone structure.[6][7]

Wikipedia's article on human height notes that average national height correlates with protein quality, and that populations with many cattle and high dairy intake were historically taller, citing the early nineteenth-century US, Argentina, New Zealand and Australia.[3] It also states that malnutrition is linked to stunted growth.[3]

Height is highly heritable (about 60 to 80 percent in twin studies), and growth in males typically finishes around 18 to 19.[3] Forum users who discuss the topic frequently point to growth plate fusion as the point after which diet is not expected to change height.[6]

The 2011 meta-analysis in the Journal of Food Protection found that pasteurisation decreased vitamins B1, B2, C and folate, that B12 and E fell and vitamin A rose qualitatively, and concluded that the effect on milk's nutritive value was minimal.[5] Wikipedia reports a 2012 Belgian review reaching a similar conclusion and notes that the FDA says pasteurisation does not destroy nutritional value.[4]
Forum posters on looksmax.org argue the opposite: one thread claims raw milk keeps vitamins, enzymes and whey protein intact and may support hormones and, in the young, height.[8]

A review of raw milk's microbiota lists Listeria, Salmonella, E. coli and Campylobacter among the organisms that can occur in it.[9] Wikipedia lists additional hazards including Brucella and tuberculosis, with children under five, people over 65, pregnant women and the immunocompromised at highest risk, and notes possible complications such as haemolytic-uremic syndrome and Guillain-Barre syndrome.[4]

Reviews have also described raw-milk transmission of tick-borne encephalitis virus and brucellosis.[10][11] The CDC and FDA strongly advise against drinking raw milk.[4] A Hacker News thread discussed reports of cats developing H5N1 infections after drinking raw milk, and Wikipedia notes H5N1 has been detected in US milk supplies.[4][12]

Wikipedia reports that about 43 US states permit some form of raw milk sale, often via farm sales or herdshares; direct sale is federally prohibited in Canada; in the UK about 150 producers sell "green top" milk directly; and it is illegal for drinking in Australia, where it is sometimes sold as bath milk.[4]

Looksmax.org threads show both enthusiasm and scepticism. Some members promote raw milk as a looksmax in its own right, others ask whether it is worthwhile, and others discuss where to obtain it.[8][13] Sceptical posters argue that bone structure is set once growth plates fuse and that raw milk and raw-food diets will not reshape the face; they recommend eating a normal healthy diet instead.[6]

No studies found on raw milk and height. Related research includes the 2011 meta-analysis of pasteurisation and vitamin levels, which also assessed advocacy claims about allergy and other outcomes.[5] A randomised trial letter examined yoghurt as an alternative to raw milk for infant eczema and allergy, which concerns allergy rather than growth.[14]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, raw milk is debated as a height and bone-structure aid, usually within broader raw-food and carnivore diet discussion.[8][6]
